title: Proactively disclose the logic of any algorithm used to determine eligibility for a public benefit
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on Civio's litigation to obtain disclosure of Spain's BOSCO algorithm. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.
decision_statement: Any algorithm a public body uses to determine eligibility for a benefit or service must have its decision logic published proactively, before a disclosure dispute arises — intellectual-property or generic security claims are not, by themselves, an adequate basis to withhold it.
decision_context: Motivated by Civio's seven-year legal fight to obtain Spain's BOSCO algorithm, which Spain's Supreme Court ultimately resolved in favour of disclosure, holding that public understanding of how administrative algorithms work is a democratic right.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Public Algorithm Transparency Board
alternatives_considered: Disclose only technical documentation, not the source code itself, as Spain's transparency council initially did.
Wait for a formal legal challenge before considering disclosure, rather than publishing proactively.

citations.title: Civio pulls back the curtain on public algorithms — Spain's Supreme Court orders the Government to release BOSCO's source code

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this litigation.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
Proactive disclosure of an eligibility algorithm's logic is a direct application of the existing transparency control — a new control would inflate the mapping without adding meaning.
Compliance must be demonstrated by an observable publication record.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether a critical algorithm could withstand a disclosure challenge.
